title: Equivariant Splitting: Self-supervised learning from incomplete data
claim: Our self-supervised method matches the supervised baseline across compression levels, while the competing self-supervised baseline degrades increasingly as compression grows.
layout: single line plot, three curves, legend box at right
description: A single wide line chart. The x-axis is compression level in percent, with ticks at 50, 60, 70, 80 and 90. The y-axis is PSNR in dB, from about 20 to 40. Three curves with markers all slope downward. The black line with x markers is Supervised. The orange line with dots is ES (Ours), and it almost exactly overlaps the supervised line. The pink or mauve line with dots is EI. It sits below the others and drops away at high compression, falling to about 20 dB at 90 percent, against about 25 dB for the other two. A boxed legend on the right names the three methods. Light gray gridlines run behind the curves. The eye goes first to the orange curve hugging the black one, then to the widening gap under the pink curve.
caption: Compressive sensing results. ES (ours) performs similarly as the supervised baseline, unlike EI (baseline) whose performance gap widens with higher compression levels.
abstract: Self-supervised learning for inverse problems allows to train a reconstruction network from noise and/or incomplete data alone. These methods have the potential of enabling learning-based solutions when obtaining ground-truth references for training is expensive or even impossible. In this paper, we propose a new self-supervised learning strategy devised for the challenging setting where measurements are observed via a single incomplete observation model. We introduce a new definition of equivariance in the context of reconstruction networks, and show that the combination of self-supervised splitting losses and equivariant reconstruction networks results in unbiased estimates of the supervised loss. Through a series of experiments on image inpainting, accelerated magnetic resonance imaging, sparse-view computed tomography, and compressive sensing, we demonstrate that the proposed loss achieves state-of-the-art performance in settings with highly rank-deficient forward models. The code is available at https://github.com/vsechaud/Equivariant-Splitting
